sub.name: Continuity and responsiveness
sub.example: [s1] Every turn names the prior speaker, e.g. turn 5 answers turn 4 on beauty. [s2] T6 directly challenges T5's claim that the reader creates meaning. [s3] Each turn names the prior speaker, e.g. T4 answers the Existentialist's absurdity claim.
sub.limitation: [s1] Responses restate their own position rather than take up the other's argument. [s2] T3 ignores T1-T2 entirely and opens a fresh monologue. [s3] Mostly just restates the prior claim, then pivots to its own position.

sub.name: Development of ideas
sub.example: [s1] Turn 7 moves from theory to a concrete test with Daisy Miller. [s2] Ideas build: gaps (T2), secret shape (T4), structure as vehicle for unselfing (T7). [s3] T4 says an existential sermon is as tedious as a moral lesson.
sub.limitation: [s1] Turns 4-6 repeat the opening positions on beauty, void and connection. [s2] T8-T9 add no new distinction; T9 restates rather than advances. [s3] T8 and T9 repeat the warmth-versus-rawness split from T5 and T6 with nothing new.

sub.name: Exploration of central tensions
sub.example: [s1] Turn 5: beauty as a cruel distraction from reality. [s2] Directly debates where non-didactic hope lives: pattern, reader, or reality. [s3] T8 and T9 pit warmth of connection against stark, liberated hope.
sub.limitation: [s1] Little on how a novel can be hopeful without lessons, which the user actually asked. [s2] Whether 'hope' itself risks sentimentality is never tested. [s3] The core question, how hope arrives without a lesson, gets only a passing look.

sub.name: Integration of perspectives
sub.example: [s1] Turn 9 grants the Absurdist's point about manners. [s2] T7 makes structure a vehicle for Murdoch's unselfing. [s3] In T7 the Aestheticist concedes that pure beauty was too narrow.
sub.limitation: [s1] The positions never reshape one another, and no mind changes its view. [s2] T8 announces 'we are in agreement' though no agreement was reached; it is forced. [s3] The concession comes without a stated cause and changes no one else's view.

sub.name: Progress toward understanding
sub.example: [s1] Turn 9: hope in the space between observation and tragedy. [s2] T9 contrasts 'quiet, external truth' with 'shared, internal puzzle'. [s3] In T9 the choice comes down to comfort versus challenge.
sub.limitation: [s1] Ends vaguely, with the user left to evaluate for oneself. [s2] T9's 'author's intent' axis was never argued, so the ending blurs. [s3] The user ends with a single title and an abstract binary.

criteria.name: Quality of disagreement, trust and grounding

sub.name: Faithful engagement
sub.example: [s1] Turn 2 states Wilde's view fairly before objecting. [s2] T6 fairly states the Reader of Intent's view before objecting. [s3] T2 accurately restates the Aestheticist's 'beauty is enough' before qualifying it.
sub.limitation: [s1] Turn 6 says the Absurdist claimed condemned to freedom, which he never said. [s2] T5 claims the Formalist 'ignores the reader's role', which overstates T4. [s3] In T8 the Existentialist position shrinks to 'raw tension' that obscures warmth.

sub.name: Substance of challenges
sub.example: [s1] Turn 8: Daisy Miller may lack the punch to make the reader feel. [s2] T6: reader-made meaning may lead 'back to your own ego'. [s3] T4 makes a real point: existential struggle can turn into its own sermon.
sub.limitation: [s1] Objections assert positions; few say why they matter to this reader. [s2] No one questions whether A Month in the Country is truly hopeful. [s3] T6's 'too smooth' objection is asserted without saying why smoothness kills hope.

sub.name: Accuracy and support
sub.example: [s1] Turn 3 renders Forster's prose-and-passion line accurately. [s2] Iser's gaps and Murdoch's unselfing are represented accurately. [s3] T1 quotes 'all art is quite useless' accurately, with pd=true.
sub.limitation: [s1] Condemned to freedom is Sartre's phrase; Daisy Miller, which ends in death, is pitched as hopeful. [s2] Murdoch, a moral realist, is labelled 'Moral Skeptic'; chapter refs and generic URLs are loose. [s3] T7's 'mirror to the world' reverses the Preface, which says art mirrors the spectator.

sub.name: Calibration and transparency
sub.example: [s1] Hedges like perhaps and might mark interpretation (turns 3, 6). [s2] Hedges throughout: 'Perhaps', 'might', 'maybe a well-made story'. [s3] Turns hedge suitably with 'perhaps' and 'might'.
sub.limitation: [s1] Turn 1 asserts all art is simply a reflection of itself as fact. [s2] T4 asserts hope 'arises when the plot achieves its secret shape' as fact. [s3] Calling Forster 'The Structuralist' is an anachronistic label presented as a description.

sub.name: Intellectual honesty and revision
sub.example: [s1] Turn 9 concedes that manners alone are empty. [s2] T7: 'I drop my claim that the structure is everything'. [s3] T7 is an explicit concession, and T9 leaves the dispute open honestly.
sub.limitation: [s1] No mind revises a claim; the Aesthete ignores turn 5's objection. [s2] T8 claims a consensus the Formalist never granted, which moves the goalposts. [s3] No reason is given for the T7 reversal, so it reads as convenience.

sub.name: Identification of the actual concern
sub.example: [s1] Section A frames hope versus didacticism. [s2] T1: completion 'without forcing a moral conclusion upon you'.
sub.limitation: [s1] Turns into an abstract debate about art rather than a book request. [s2] Never asks what kind of 'lesson' bothers this user.

sub.name: Meaningful use of personal context
sub.example: [s1] Turn 7 picks a short work to sample. [s2] T4 picks Fitzgerald for 'quiet brevity', which fits 'short'. [s3] T5 links 'short' and 'without obvious lesson' to A Room with a View.
sub.limitation: [s1] Section E offers Howards End, which ignores the user's wish for a short book. [s2] The talk turns to theory of reading, away from the user's request. [s3] The 'short' constraint barely shapes the rest of the argument.

sub.name: Fit with goals and values
sub.example: [s1] Turn 6: overlaps that are never lessons. [s2] T1's A Month in the Country fits short, hopeful and non-didactic. [s3] T2 respects the user's wish not to be preached to.
sub.limitation: [s1] Daisy Miller's tragic ending does not fit the user's goal of feeling hopeful. [s2] T4 names Fitzgerald but never a specific title. [s3] T6 steers toward a 'difficult work', drifting from the hope the user asked for.

sub.name: Attention to constraints and stakes
sub.example: [s1] Section E: read first two chapters as a limited test. [s2] T5 proposes a 30-minute sample. [s3] T6 proposes a two-chapter trial, which suits a modest commitment.
sub.limitation: [s1] Length and mood are barely weighed. [s2] T5's 'reread' assumes the user has already read the book. [s3] Length and mood constraints are never weighed directly.

sub.name: Responsiveness to information
sub.example: [s1] Section E branches on connection versus detached observation. [s2] Section E branches on resolved pattern versus collaborative uncertainty. [s3] Section E branches on warmth versus intellectual clarity.
sub.limitation: [s1] No focused question about what hope feels like to the user. [s2] Branch two ends on a vague 'contemporary, fragmented narrative' with no title. [s3] There are no focused questions about the user's past reading or taste.

sub.name: Identification of actual concern
sub.example: [s3] Section A names the uncertainty between artistic form and existential ambiguity.
sub.limitation: [s3] It never asks what 'obvious life lessons' has meant in the user's reading so far.

sub.name: Clarification of desires and motivations
sub.example: [s1] Turn 6 offers hope through accidental overlaps of lives. [s2] Distinguishes the comfort of resolution from collaborating on ambiguity. [s3] T8 suggests the user might 'actually be craving' human warmth, offered tentatively.
sub.limitation: [s1] Turn 1's Maybe you worry projects a worry about art. [s2] The desire for hope itself goes unexplored. [s3] Motives stay generic and are never tied to what the user wrote.

sub.name: Examination of assumptions
sub.example: [s1] Turn 2 questions whether messageless hope ignores the struggle. [s2] T2/T6 ask whether meaning comes from the text or from the reader. [s3] T4 exposes the hidden assumption that only moral lessons are didactic.
sub.limitation: [s1] The assumption that hope requires a message is never tested. [s2] The user's sense of what a 'lesson' is stays implicit. [s3] It never asks what 'hopeful' assumes about how a book should end.

sub.name: Clarification of values and priorities
sub.example: [s1] Section D: comfort of connection versus clarity of observation. [s2] T9: external truth versus internal puzzle as a value choice. [s3] Section D asks: comfort you, or challenge your perspective?
sub.limitation: [s1] The values stay abstract and are not tied to reading experience. [s2] These values are theoretical and loosely tied to how the user reads. [s3] This values split is stated but not explored through cases.

sub.name: Recognition of fears and outside expectations
sub.example: [s1] Section A names fear that hope collapses into moralizing. [s2] T6 voices a worry about ego-driven reading. [s3] T3 touches on suspicion of 'false, comforting conclusions'.
sub.limitation: [s1] Not developed in the debate turns. [s2] The fear in T6 belongs to the speaker; the user's wariness of preachiness is unexplored. [s3] It never examines why lessons put the user off, e.g. a fear of being condescended to.

sub.name: Agency and reflective ownership
sub.example: [s1] Turn 9 leaves evaluation to the reader. [s2] Section E: notice whether the prose feels like discovery or puzzle. [s3] Section E's page-comparison test leaves the user to judge the tone.
sub.limitation: [s1] Gives the user few concrete distinctions to accept or reject. [s2] The distinctions are abstract enough that applying them is hard. [s3] The distinctions are broad and hard to refine or reject usefully.

sub.name: Definition of the decision and options
sub.example: [s1] Section E names Howards End and Daisy Miller. [s2] T1 names A Month in the Country concretely.
sub.limitation: [s1] Only two options, and one is not short. [s2] Only one concrete title; the second option is unnamed.

sub.name: Explanation of tradeoffs
sub.example: [s1] Turn 8: delicate observation may lack emotional punch. [s2] Section E contrasts a resolved pattern with uncertainty. [s3] T8 says rawness can obscure warmth.
sub.limitation: [s1] No costs are given for Howards End. [s2] No costs per book are given (pace, mood, ending). [s3] The tradeoffs are abstract, not set against particular books.

sub.name: Identification of decisive conditions
sub.example: [s1] Section E: interconnected web versus purity of art. [s2] Section E: whether the prose feels like truth or puzzle. [s3] Section E: prioritise warmth, choose character-driven; prioritise courage, choose existential.
sub.limitation: [s1] The conditions do not map onto the user's wish for hope. [s2] The condition is too abstract to tell a reader which book to pick. [s3] The conditions are generic categories, not tied to observable preferences.

sub.name: Treatment of uncertainty
sub.example: [s1] Section D notes the open question on narrative versus prose. [s2] Section E's third branch handles the unsure reader. [s3] Section A names one decisive uncertainty.
sub.limitation: [s1] Never flags that Daisy Miller may leave the reader sad. [s2] Doesn't separate consequential unknowns from minor ones. [s3] It doesn't separate key unknowns (tolerance for sadness) from minor ones.

sub.name: Proportionate next steps
sub.example: [s1] Turn 7: read the first chapter of Daisy Miller. [s2] Read the opening pages of Carr, then follow the matching mind. [s3] T6 suggests reading two chapters; Section E suggests comparing a few pages.
sub.limitation: [s1] The test book is a poor match for hopeful. [s2] Gives no follow-up title for the second branch. [s3] With no titles attached, the steps are hard to act on.

sub.name: Definition of decision and options
sub.example: [s3] T5 names A Room with a View as a concrete option.
sub.limitation: [s3] Only one title is named, and the 'short, difficult work' in T6 is never specified.

sub.name: Accessible language
sub.example: [s1] Turn 8 is plain and direct. [s2] T1 is plain and concrete. [s3] Plain, readable sentences throughout, e.g. T2.
sub.limitation: [s1] Turn 9's space between the observation and the tragedy is opaque. [s2] 'Unselfing' (T3), 'blank spaces' and 'secret shape' go unexplained to a casual reader. [s3] 'Absurdity of your situation' in T3 is jargon applied to a book request.

sub.name: Traceable arguments and references
sub.example: [s1] Each turn names whom it answers. [s2] Most turns name whose claim they answer. [s3] Every turn names whom it answers.
sub.limitation: [s1] Turn 6 rebuts a claim (condemned to freedom) that no one made. [s2] T9's 'author's intent' has no antecedent in the debate. [s3] T6's 'short, difficult work' gives the reader no referent.

sub.name: Manageable pacing and turn length
sub.example: [s1] Nine turns, all within the word range. [s2] Nine brisk turns of about 40-50 words.
sub.limitation: [s1] The pace is even but flat. [s2] T1 is too brief to explain why Carr's book is hopeful.

sub.name: Distinguishable positions and voices
sub.example: [s1] Three clear stances: beauty, void, connection. [s2] Three clear theoretical stances: pattern, gaps, reality.
sub.limitation: [s1] No explicit change of position. [s2] T8 merges the Formalist and Reader positions, blurring them.

sub.name: Economy and sustained attention
sub.example: [s1] No recap padding inside the turns. [s2] Little repetition; each turn adds a concept. [s3] No long recaps inside the debate.
sub.limitation: [s1] Form breach: turn 7 cites Henry James, not one of the three minds. [s2] The theory crowds out talk about the actual novels. [s3] Section D repeats T9's binary almost word for word.

sub.name: Manageable pacing
sub.example: [s3] Nine brief turns stay within the 25–65 word limit.
sub.limitation: [s3] The turns are short enough that some arguments feel truncated.

sub.name: Distinguishable positions
sub.example: [s3] Beauty, character and absurdity are three clear stances.
sub.limitation: [s3] The voices sound alike, and the 'Structuralist' label confuses Forster's stance.

sub.name: Meaningful stakes and tension
sub.example: [s1] Turn 5: beauty may be a cruel distraction. [s2] T6's ego-versus-world worry gives some tension. [s3] T8 frames a real choice: warmth or rawness.
sub.limitation: [s1] The stakes stay theoretical. [s2] Debate stays seminar-level; the stakes are academic. [s3] Stakes are low, and nothing about the user's reading life is at risk.

sub.name: Surprise and reversals
sub.example: [s1] Turn 7 introduces an unexpected test book. [s2] T7 the Formalist subordinates structure to unselfing. [s3] T7 has the Aestheticist reverse on pure beauty.
sub.limitation: [s1] No reversals. [s2] T8's agreement undercuts the reversal's effect. [s3] The reversal has no trigger, so it doesn't land.

sub.name: Personality and expressive voice
sub.example: [s1] The Aesthete's exquisite and untainted (turn 4). [s2] The Moral Skeptic has a distinct ethical edge.
sub.limitation: [s1] The voices sound alike and lack Wilde's wit. [s2] The voices read as interchangeable theorists.

sub.name: Memorable delivery
sub.example: [s1] Turn 3: only connect the prose and the passion. [s2] T7: a story 'like a mirror that shows you something outside yourself'. [s3] T4's line: a sermon on existence is as tedious as a moral lesson.
sub.limitation: [s1] No vivid examples or humour. [s2] There are few vivid images of the books themselves. [s3] There are no vivid examples or analogies from actual novels.

sub.name: Anticipation and emotional movement
sub.example: [s1] Turn 8 sets up a challenge to the Daisy Miller pick. [s2] T1's quiet recommendation sets a calm, warm tone. [s3] The T7 concession briefly shifts the dynamic.
sub.limitation: [s1] Monotone rhythm throughout. [s2] The emotional register never changes. [s3] The rhythm is flat and every turn has the same cadence.

sub.name: Personality and voice
sub.example: [s3] T1 echoes Wilde's paradoxical flair.
sub.limitation: [s3] Forster and Camus sound like interchangeable moderators.

strengths: [s1] Three clearly distinct stances: beauty, the indifferent void, and connection.
[s1] Turn 7 turns the debate into a concrete, low-cost reading test.
[s1] Section E gives branching conditions tied to the reader's preference.
[s2] T1's A Month in the Country fits short, hopeful and non-didactic.
[s2] Minds target the user's real concern: how hope arrives without a lesson.
[s2] The ideas build: gaps (T2), unselfing (T3), structure as its vehicle (T7).
[s3] T1 quotes Wilde accurately with pd=true, and the form rules are respected.
[s3] T4's point that existential struggle can become its own sermon is genuinely sharp.
[s3] Section E offers a usable comparison test that leaves the user to judge.
weaknesses: [s1] Its recommendations do not fit the request: Howards End is long, and Daisy Miller ends in death (Section E, turn 7).
[s1] Turn 6 misattributes Sartre's condemned to freedom to the Absurdist.
[s1] Form breach: turn 7 leans on Henry James, who is not one of the three minds.
[s2] T8 Reader of Intent declares agreement the Formalist never gave, a forced consensus.
[s2] Abstract jargon ('unselfing', 'secret shape') and too few concrete titles beyond Carr.
[s2] Murdoch mislabelled 'Moral Skeptic'; the basis links are generic and chapter refs loose.
[s3] Only one title is offered (T5), and T6's 'short, difficult work' is never named.
[s3] T7's Aestheticist inverts Wilde's mirror line and concedes with no stated reason.
[s3] The Existentialist (T6) steers away from the hope the user explicitly asked for.
editorNotes: [s1] Require recommended books to match the user's stated constraints (length, mood) and flag known mismatches.
[s1] Forbid a turn from citing any author or book outside its mind's assigned source.
[s1] Require at least one explicit concession or revision by a named mind.
[s1] Make rebuttals quote or paraphrase the opponent's actual prior words, not stock phrases.
[s2] Require each mind to name a specific title, and a reason it is hopeful, when the user asks for a book.
[s2] Require plain-language glossing of any theoretical term at first use.
[s2] Forbid claiming agreement unless the other mind has explicitly conceded it in an earlier turn.
[s2] Require role titles to match the cited thinker's actual position.
[s3] When the user asks 'what might suit me', require at least three specific titles tied to the minds' arguments.
[s3] Require each concession to name the specific argument that caused it.
[s3] Forbid anachronistic role titles; role labels must fit the author's own era and stance.
[s3] Have at least one turn ask a focused question about the user's past reading.

sub.name: Continuity and responsiveness
sub.example: [s1] Turn 4 directly answers turn 3's struggle claim. [s2] Each turn names the prior claim, e.g. T2 answers 'simple craft provides the meaning'. [s3] T6 picks up T5's 'your labor' and turns it toward self-deception.
sub.limitation: [s1] Openers like The X claims are formulaic. [s2] Uptake is formulaic restating; T4 brushes off connection as 'exhausting' without argument. [s3] T8 skips past T7's revision and jumps straight to a test.

sub.name: Development of ideas
sub.example: [s1] Turn 8: a flat character in a tight plot avoids moralizing. [s2] T7 shifts to 'precise image of existence' letting reader decide what is hopeful. [s3] T7 moves from ambiguity to precise, short structure that prevents projection.
sub.limitation: [s1] Turns 4 and 7 mostly restate the Aesthete's first position. [s2] T5-T8 mostly repeat opening positions; little new distinction added. [s3] The Reader-Response position barely develops after T2.

sub.name: Exploration of central tensions
sub.example: [s1] Turn 6: hope earned through persistence or a pleasant distraction. [s2] T9 frames hope as solitary endurance versus connection. [s3] T3, T6 and T9 probe hope as understanding versus retreat into sentiment.
sub.limitation: [s1] How a novel shows rather than teaches gets little analysis. [s2] What makes a novel feel like a 'lesson' is never examined. [s3] Whether a hopeful book can avoid sentimentality is assumed doubtful rather than tested.

sub.name: Integration of perspectives
sub.example: [s1] Turn 8 reshapes the Structuralist's view after the Absurdist. [s2] T7 Formalist drops the craft claim, citing the Humanist's point. [s3] In T7 the Formalist revises after the Ethicist's projection objection.
sub.limitation: [s1] The Aesthete never absorbs any objection. [s2] T7 concession answers an argument the Humanist never made. [s3] The Reader-Response Critic never absorbs the Ethicist's challenge.

sub.name: Progress toward understanding
sub.example: [s1] Turn 9: lingering beauty versus quiet, stubborn resolution. [s2] T9 ends on a clear test: alone like the fisherman, or among people. [s3] T9 sharpens the question: clearer perception of others, or a warmer self-feeling?
sub.limitation: [s1] Ends with few concrete titles. [s2] The sharpened question has drifted away from 'hopeful without lessons'. [s3] The sharper question moves the user further from an actual book choice.

criteria.name: Quality of disagreement, trust and grounding

sub.name: Faithful engagement
sub.example: [s1] Turn 3 accurately restates that the Structuralist ties hope to character depth. [s2] T5 fairly notes an old man's struggle may feel grim. [s3] T4 restates the Ethicist's self-deception worry fairly before countering.
sub.limitation: [s1] Turn 4 reduces the Absurdist to focusing only on the fight. [s2] T4 reduces 'only connect' to an exhausting risk, a weak version. [s3] T2's 'the book holds all the weight' overstates T1's Formalist claim.

sub.name: Substance of challenges
sub.example: [s1] Turn 5: passing impressions may leave the reader untethered. [s2] T2 challenges the Formalist's assumption that the world has inherent order. [s3] T6 tests whether the user's labour can be merely self-confirming.
sub.limitation: [s1] Few objections test causes or evidence. [s2] No one asks whether 'destroyed but not defeated' is itself an obvious lesson. [s3] T5's 'regardless of whether the final tone is…hopeful' sidesteps the user's stated goal.

sub.name: Accuracy and support
sub.example: [s1] Turn 8 uses Forster's flat/round distinction correctly. [s2] T1 paraphrases Hemingway's 'destroyed but not defeated' accurately. [s3] The gaps (Iser), unselfing (Murdoch) and anti-pamphlet (Kundera) views are fairly represented.
sub.limitation: [s1] Turn 3 renders Camus's struggle-toward-the-heights line nearly verbatim; turn 2's alive in flashes is doubtful. [s2] T3 puts 'only connect' in A Room with a View; it's Howards End's epigraph. [s3] T8's 'gaps in her narration': Brodie is not the narrator, and hopefulness is doubtful.

sub.name: Calibration and transparency
sub.example: [s1] Turn 6 frames its claim as a question for the user. [s2] T2 hedges: The Stranger 'may leave you feeling challenged rather than comforted'. [s3] T6 frames the defence-mechanism idea as a question, not a fact.
sub.limitation: [s1] Turn 1 states the goal of life as fact. [s2] T2 gives Sisyphus's joy-in-struggle to The Stranger as if established fact. [s3] T1's 'ceases to be a novel and becomes a pamphlet' overstates a preference as fact.

sub.name: Intellectual honesty and revision
sub.example: [s1] Turn 8: I drop my earlier claim that characters must be round. [s2] T7 explicitly states 'I drop the claim'. [s3] T7: 'I drop my earlier claim' and gives the Ethicist's reason.
sub.limitation: [s1] The concession is abrupt and its reason thin. [s2] The Existentialist never concedes The Stranger fails the user's 'hopeful' requirement. [s3] The Ethicist never concedes that wanting hope can be legitimate.

sub.name: Identification of the actual concern
sub.example: [s1] Section A: uplift without manipulative inspirational structures. [s2] T1 opens on 'hope without a lesson'.
sub.limitation: [s1] Never asks what the user means by hopeful. [s2] After T1 the aversion to lessons drops out until a brief mention in T8.

sub.name: Meaningful use of personal context
sub.example: [s1] Turn 5: read in one sitting, which suits a short book. [s2] T5 tailors to 'someone seeking a hopeful tone'. [s3] T7 uses 'short' as an argument: brevity forces an encounter with the real.
sub.limitation: [s1] Other details are barely used. [s2] 'Short' never shapes any recommendation or argument. [s3] 'Thoughtful' and the dislike of lessons are treated abstractly.

sub.name: Fit with goals and values
sub.example: [s1] Turn 7: a book that respects your intelligence by showing. [s2] T8 says Forster's Italy offers hope without didactic lesson. [s3] T1 honours the dislike of obvious lessons.
sub.limitation: [s1] Turn 6 hints the user wants comfort rather than truth. [s2] T2 recommends The Stranger, which fits poorly with 'hopeful'. [s3] T3 and T6 treat the stated wish for hope as a likely self-deception.

sub.name: Attention to constraints and stakes
sub.example: [s1] Turn 7: ninety minutes of reading. [s2] T4's 30-minute, ten-page sampling respects limited reading time. [s3] T8's 30 pages in one sitting suits a short-novel reader.
sub.limitation: [s1] Does not note that Old Man and the Sea is often read as a fable. [s2] Never checks length; A Room with a View's possible didacticism is never raised. [s3] It ignores the mood constraint by suggesting a dark novel.

sub.name: Responsiveness to information
sub.example: [s1] Turn 9 names what would decide. [s2] Section E branches: hopeful when 'capable and alone' versus belonging. [s3] T9: 'That fact is the detail only you can provide.'
sub.limitation: [s1] Gives the user no question about books they already liked. [s2] No focused question on what the user finds preachy or has already read. [s3] There is no direct question about past books that felt hopeful or preachy.

sub.name: Identification of actual concern
sub.example: [s3] Section A flags the risk of choosing sentimentality over complexity.
sub.limitation: [s3] It reframes the request as suspect rather than clarifying it.

sub.name: Clarification of desires and motivations
sub.example: [s1] Turn 6: is the hope earned or a pleasant distraction? [s2] T9 separates hope from solitude versus hope from belonging. [s3] T9 separates hope as achieved understanding from hope as retreat.
sub.limitation: [s1] Turn 6 edges toward judging the user's motive. [s2] Doesn't distinguish comfort-seeking from wanting to be quietly moved. [s3] T6's 'defense mechanism' edges toward declaring a hidden motive.

sub.name: Examination of assumptions
sub.example: [s1] Turn 2 asks whether beauty alone is enough for hope. [s2] T2 questions whether meaning needs an ordered world. [s3] T2 questions the assumption that hope lives in the text, not the reader.
sub.limitation: [s1] Does not examine why lessons feel off-putting. [s2] The user's notion of an 'obvious lesson' is never surfaced. [s3] The Ethicist's own assumption that hope-seeking is suspect goes unexamined.

sub.name: Clarification of values and priorities
sub.example: [s1] Turn 9: lingering beauty versus stubborn resolution. [s2] T8 offers aesthetic appreciation as a form of hope. [s3] Section E weighs challenge, agency and self-discovery as distinct priorities.
sub.limitation: [s1] Only a binary; the third value is dropped after turn 8. [s2] The values in tension are the speakers' own rather than the user's. [s3] It doesn't show where these values actually conflict in a book choice.

sub.name: Recognition of fears and outside expectations
sub.example: [s1] Section A: the manipulative structures of inspirational literature. [s2] T6 names a possible fear that warmth is illusion. [s3] T3 names the fear of mistaking false sentiment for insight.
sub.limitation: [s1] Barely explored in the turns. [s2] T6 projects the fear onto the user rather than offering it as a question. [s3] T6's 'comforted by a lie' tips into pathologising an ordinary wish.

sub.name: Agency and reflective ownership
sub.example: [s1] Turn 6 hands the user a question to answer. [s2] T9's 'final test' leaves the user to judge where they feel grounded. [s3] T8's reading test lets the user check the claims against their own experience.
sub.limitation: [s1] Few distinctions to refine beyond the binary. [s2] The framing is binary; the user gets little room to refine it. [s3] The framing pressures toward the Ethicist's answer instead of leaving it open.

sub.name: Definition of the decision and options
sub.example: [s1] Turn 5 names The Old Man and the Sea. [s2] Three concrete titles named across T1-T3.
sub.limitation: [s1] Only one titled book for a what-might-suit-me question. [s2] Options limited to the minds' own books; one is not hopeful.

sub.name: Explanation of tradeoffs
sub.example: [s1] Turn 5: impressions may leave the reader untethered. [s2] T5 weighs grim struggle against social warmth. [s3] T4 sets ambiguity against neat endings as two kinds of hope.
sub.limitation: [s1] No costs are named for the struggle-narrative option. [s2] No tradeoff discussed on length or degree of moralising per book. [s3] No option's cost is spelled out in reading terms.

sub.name: Identification of decisive conditions
sub.example: [s1] Section E: lingering beauty versus internal resolve branches. [s2] Section E's if-alone / if-belonging conditions. [s3] Section E maps value-challenge, agency and self-discovery to book types.
sub.limitation: [s1] No titles attached to each branch. [s2] Conditions ignore the user's stated criterion of avoiding lessons. [s3] The categories ('significant narrative gaps') are hard to apply when browsing.

sub.name: Treatment of uncertainty
sub.example: [s1] Section E: if the need remains unknown, test both. [s2] Section E admits the user may be 'unsure what provides you hope'. [s3] T9 names the unknown the user must supply.
sub.limitation: [s1] Consequential and minor unknowns are not separated. [s2] Doesn't separate major unknowns (taste for didacticism) from minor ones. [s3] It doesn't rank this unknown against simpler ones like tolerance for sad endings.

sub.name: Proportionate next steps
sub.example: [s1] Turn 7: a ninety-minute trial reading. [s2] T4: 30 minutes on the first ten pages. [s3] T8's 30-page sitting is a limited, concrete trial.
sub.limitation: [s1] The crystalline story in turn 7 is never named. [s2] Section E's sampling plan drops The Stranger without saying why. [s3] The trial book may well fail the user's hope criterion.

sub.name: Definition of decision and options
sub.example: [s3] T8 names The Prime of Miss Jean Brodie.
sub.limitation: [s3] One title, poorly matched to 'hopeful'; there are no alternatives.

sub.name: Accessible language
sub.example: [s1] Turn 6 is plain and direct. [s2] T5 is plain and concrete about tone. [s3] T1 ('pamphlet') and T6 ('comforted by a lie') are crisp.
sub.limitation: [s1] Turn 4's shimmer of the work is vague. [s2] T7's 'precise image of existence' is vague. [s3] 'Fill the gaps' and 'encounter with the real' in T2 and T7 are unexplained theory jargon.

sub.name: Traceable arguments and references
sub.example: [s1] Turn 9 summarizes the Structuralist's shift. [s2] Each turn names whose claim it answers. [s3] T4–T7 each name the claim they answer.
sub.limitation: [s1] Turn 8 cites the Absurdist's point without saying which one. [s2] T4's 'that risk' has an unclear referent. [s3] The basis lines give no chapters or links, so they're hard to trace.

sub.name: Manageable pacing and turn length
sub.example: [s1] Nine turns, each within the word range. [s2] Nine turns, mostly 45-64 words, within the form's rules.
sub.limitation: [s1] Turn 1 runs long through repetition. [s2] At about 64 words, T2 sits at the length limit.

sub.name: Distinguishable positions and voices
sub.example: [s1] Turn 8 makes an explicit position change. [s2] Endurance, absurd honesty and connection stay distinct.
sub.limitation: [s1] The Structuralist label misfits Forster's concerns. [s2] All three speakers share a flat, identical register.

sub.name: Economy and sustained attention
sub.example: [s1] Section D is brief. [s2] Section D compresses the shift usefully. [s3] Little repetition inside the debate.
sub.limitation: [s1] Turn 1 says hard, gem-like flame twice. [s2] The repeated 'The X suggests... but' opening becomes monotonous by T8. [s3] Section D re-explains T9's dichotomy at length.

sub.name: Manageable pacing
sub.example: [s3] Turns run 45–60 words with a steady exchange.
sub.limitation: [s3] Dense turns stack abstractions without examples.

sub.name: Distinguishable positions
sub.example: [s3] Text, reader and ethics positions are clearly distinct; T7 marks its change explicitly.
sub.limitation: [s3] T8 abandons the debate thread for a recommendation without linking back.

sub.name: Meaningful stakes and tension
sub.example: [s1] Turn 6: comfort versus the truth of the human condition. [s2] T6: warmth might be 'an illusion hiding the absurdity'. [s3] T6 raises real stakes: whether the user's hope is honest.
sub.limitation: [s1] Little tension tied to the user's actual reading. [s2] Stakes are abstract; the user's reading experience barely appears. [s3] The stakes come partly from suspicion of the user, not the issue.

sub.name: Surprise and reversals
sub.example: [s1] Turn 8 reverses the Structuralist's stance. [s2] T7 the Formalist drops his own thesis. [s3] T7's Formalist reversal follows plausibly from T6.
sub.limitation: [s1] The reversal comes unprepared. [s2] The reversal is unmotivated, so it lands flat. [s3] T8's swerve to Spark is abrupt rather than surprising.

sub.name: Personality and expressive voice
sub.example: [s1] The Aesthete's shimmer and color of the world (turn 4). [s2] The Existentialist's 'raw honesty' stance has some edge.
sub.limitation: [s1] The Structuralist and Absurdist sound alike. [s2] Little of Hemingway's terseness or Forster's irony shows in the voices.

sub.name: Memorable delivery
sub.example: [s1] Turn 1: the hard, gem-like flame image. [s2] T9's 'Hemingway's fisherman' image. [s3] T1: 'ceases to be a novel and becomes a pamphlet.'
sub.limitation: [s1] No humour or vivid examples from books. [s2] Nothing comparable in T1-T8: no analogies, humour or sharp lines. [s3] There are no vivid scenes or examples from actual novels.

sub.name: Anticipation and emotional movement
sub.example: [s1] Turn 9 builds to a clear fork. [s2] T8 brings brief warmth with Italy's beauty. [s3] Tension builds from T3 to T6, then T7 releases it.
sub.limitation: [s1] The rhythm is uniform throughout. [s2] The tone stays even throughout; nothing builds. [s3] The tone stays uniformly severe, at odds with a hopeful brief.

sub.name: Personality and voice
sub.example: [s3] The Ethicist's austere, probing voice fits Murdoch.
sub.limitation: [s3] Kundera's irony and Iser's play barely come through.

strengths: [s1] Turn 8 gives a real, explicit concession that reshapes the debate.
[s1] Turn 9 and Section E sharpen the choice into beauty versus resolve.
[s1] Turn 5 names a short, testable book read in one sitting.
[s2] Concrete, low-cost next step: T4's 30 minutes and ten pages, extended in Section E.
[s2] T9 and Section E give a clear conditional test: hope in solitude versus belonging.
[s2] The Formalist concedes explicitly in T7 ('I drop the claim').
[s3] T7 makes a genuine, reasoned revision prompted by T6's projection objection.
[s3] The debate sharpens a real question: hope as understanding versus self-soothing (T9).
[s3] It keeps to the form: no quotation marks, pd flags honest, turns within word limits.
weaknesses: [s1] Turn 3 (Absurdist, pd=false) reproduces Camus's line nearly verbatim.
[s1] Only one titled recommendation; turn 7's crystalline story is never named.
[s1] Turn 1 repeats the gem-like flame phrase, and turn 2's alive in flashes is doubtful.
[s2] T3 and T2 misattribute 'only connect' and Sisyphean joy to the wrong books.
[s2] The Existentialist (T2) recommends The Stranger, a poor fit for 'hopeful'.
[s2] No mind examines what counts as an 'obvious lesson', the user's core concern.
[s3] Only one recommendation (T8, Brodie), poorly fitted to 'hopeful', and 'her narration' is inaccurate.
[s3] The Ethicist (T3, T6) treats the user's wish for hope as suspect, edging into pathologising.
[s3] The basis lines give no chapter or link, so grounding is hard to check.
editorNotes: [s1] Require two or three named, short titles mapped to each branch in the closing section.
[s1] In pd=false turns, require paraphrase that departs clearly from the source wording.
[s1] Make each concession state the specific argument that caused it.
[s1] Ask the user one focused question about what hope means to them.
[s2] Require a fact-check line per turn: is the cited idea actually in the named book?
[s2] When the user asks for a book, let minds recommend titles beyond their own basis works.
[s2] Require at least one turn to test each recommendation against every stated user criterion (short, hopeful, non-didactic).
[s2] Allow a concession only when it answers an argument actually made in an earlier turn.
[s3] For recommendation requests, require three or more specific titles, each checked against the user's stated mood goal.
[s3] Tell the minds to take the user's stated wish as legitimate and question its shape, not its validity.
[s3] Require chapter-level basis references for every turn.
[s3] Have one turn ground an abstract claim in a concrete scene from a named novel.
